Given that $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers greater than 0 such that
$\bullet\ c=3a+1$
$\bullet\ a+b+c=15$
prove, by exhaustion, that the product $abc$ is always a multiple of 4
You may use the table below to illustrate your answer.
(3)

parts.text:

$\bullet\ c=3a+1$
$\bullet\ a+b+c=15$
prove, by exhaustion, that the product $abc$ is always a multiple of 4
You may use the table below to illustrate your answer.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
Main method: Numerical solution finding all known solutions
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline a & b & c & abc\\ \hline 1 & 10 & 4 & 40\\ \hline 2 & 6 & 7 & 84\\ \hline 3 & 2 & 10 & 60\\ \hline\end{array}$
B1: Any correct set of values for $a$, $b$ and $c$. You can ignore any attempt at the product $abc$
M1: Any two fully correct rows including the correct calculations for the products. Condone extra/incorrect rows
A1: Fully correct. The solution must have the three correct rows with correct calculations for $abc$; any extra (or incorrect) rows must be deleted or somehow excluded; a minimal statement showing that they are aware that 40, 84 and 60 are multiples of 4, e.g. they are all divisible by 4, use of a tick, prove, QED, calculations such as $\frac{40}{4}=10$. They can be divided by 4 (on its own) is insufficient without further clarification such as "to give whole numbers"; no incorrect calculations.
Alt 1: Via deduction
B1: Either solves $a+b+c=15$ with $c=3a+1$ to conclude that $4a+b=14$ o.e. and states that $b$ is even, or uses $c=3a+1$ to state that if $a$ is odd then $c$ is even and if $a$ is even then $c$ is odd
M1: Attempts to generalise and offers one of the two possibilities for the product $abc$. Either states then when $a$ is odd, $b$ is even and $c$ is even, therefore $abc=$ odd$\times$even$\times$even $=$ multiple of 4, Or states then when $a$ is even, $b$ is even and $c$ is odd, therefore $abc=$ even$\times$even$\times$odd $=$ multiple of 4
A1: Fully correct. The solution must have the two possible "calculations" for $abc$; no incorrect "calculations". E.g. if they state that even$\times$even is a multiple of 4 because $2n\times 2n=4n^2$ it is A0. It must be along the lines of $2m\times 2n=4mn$ with different variables.
You may see a hybrid solution that can be marked along similar lines. If you see a tabular solution and one via deduction, award marks for the better one.

- All values of $abc$ are multiples of 4. One correct set $a$, $b$ & $c$ B1; Two correct rows M1; Fully correct + statement A1

- You may see a hybrid solution that can be marked along similar lines. Mark positively.
- Please use review if you are uncertain.

In this question you must show all stages of your working.
Solutions relying on calculator technology are not acceptable.
$\mathrm{f}(x)=4x^3+ax^2-29x+b$
where $a$ and $b$ are constants.
Given that $(2x+1)$ is a factor of $\mathrm{f}(x)$,

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) show that
$a+4b=-56$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
Sets $\mathrm{f}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=0\rightarrow4\times\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^3+a\times\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2-29\times\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+b=0$
M1
$\Rightarrow\frac{1}{4}a+b+14=0\Rightarrow a+4b=-56$ *
A1*
M1: Attempts to set $\mathrm{f}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=0\rightarrow$ equation in $a$ and $b$. Condone slips (e.g. on signs) but $\mathrm{f}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=0$ is M0. Score when you see embedded values within the equation or two correct terms on the lhs of the equation.
A1*: Completes proof with at least one intermediate simplified and correct line such as $\frac{1}{4}a+b+14=0$. Simplifying each term is sufficient $-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}a+\frac{29}{2}+b=0$. Any incorrect lines written after the start of their 'proof' should be scored A0*
Solutions where the $=0$ is implied but not stated should be awarded M1 A0*
E.g. $\mathrm{f}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=4\times\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^3+a\times\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2-29\times\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+b=\frac{1}{4}a+b+14$. So $\frac{1}{4}a+b=-14\Rightarrow a+4b=-56$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- If you cannot see what they are doing and find it hard to award, then put in review please

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Given also that when $\mathrm{f}(x)$ is divided by $(x-2)$ the remainder is $-25$
(b) find a second simplified equation linking $a$ and $b$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
Sets $\mathrm{f}(2)=-25\rightarrow4\times2^3+a\times2^2-29\times2+b=-25$
M1
$4a+b=1$
A1
M1: Attempts to set $\mathrm{f}(2)=-25\rightarrow$ equation in $a$ and $b$. Condone slips, e.g. sign slips or setting $\mathrm{f}(2)=25$. Setting $\mathrm{f}(-2)=-25$ is not a slip and should be marked M0.
A1: $4a+b=1$ or other simplified equivalent such as $a+\frac{1}{4}b-\frac{1}{4}=0$. The constant terms must be collected. Note that this is not a given answer so allow recovery.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Example of a long division method for (b). When $\mathrm{f}(x)=4x^3+ax^2-29x+b$ is divided by $(x-2)$ the remainder is $-25$. Quotient $4x^2+(a+8)x+(2a-13)$; $4x^3-8x^2$; $(a+8)x^2-29x$; $(a+8)x^2-(2a+16)x$; $(2a-13)x+b$; $(2a-13)x+(-4a+26)$; $b+4a-26$. Remainder is $-25$ so $b+4a-26=-25\Rightarrow b+4a=1$

parts.label: c
parts.text:

(i) find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$,
(ii) fully factorise $\mathrm{f}(x)$.
(5)

(i) Solves $a+4b=-56$ with their $4a+b=1\Rightarrow a=\ldots,b=\ldots$
M1
$a=4, b=-15$
A1
(ii) $4x^3+4x^2-29x-15=(2x+1)(2x^2+x-15)$
M1, A1
$=(2x+1)(2x-5)(x+3)$ cso
A1
(c)(i) M1: Attempts to solve $a+4b=-56$ (allowing for slips) with their $4a+b=1\Rightarrow a=\ldots,b=\ldots$. Award as long as values appear for both $a$ and $b$, so allow these just written down (say from a calculator). There is no need for their calculations.
A1: Both values correct: $a=4, b=-15$. Both just written down without working scores M1 A1 provided (b) is correct
(c)(ii) M1: Attempt to divide or factorise out $(2x+1)$ from their $4x^3+4x^2-29x-15$ or multiple thereof. For factorisation look for correct first and last terms E.g. $4x^3+"a"x^2-29x+"b"=(2x+1)(2x^2+kx\pm"b")$. questions.question_text:
(i) (a) Find, in ascending powers of $x$, the 2nd, 3rd and 5th terms of the binomial expansion of
$(3+2x)^6$
(3)
For a particular value of $x$, these three terms form consecutive terms in a geometric series.
(b) Find this value of $x$.
(3)
(ii) In a different geometric series,
$\bullet$ the first term is $\sin^2\theta$
$\bullet$ the common ratio is $2\cos\theta$
$\bullet$ the sum to infinity is $\frac{8}{5}$
(a) Show that
$5\cos^2\theta-16\cos\theta+3=0$
(3)
(b) Hence find the exact value of the 2nd term in the series.
(3)

A1
M1: For an attempt at using the binomial expansion to find one of the required terms. Condone the omission of the brackets on the $2x$ terms. Allow using combination notation. Don't be concerned over any labelling (2nd term). May be awarded from a full expansion
A1: Any two correct terms, simplified or not. The $^6C_2$ must now be numerical. Don't be concerned by labelling and accept as part of a large list or expansion
A1: All three terms correct and simplified. They may be part of a larger or complete expansion, which is fine. Look for the 2nd, 3rd and 5th terms. Accept the 3 terms with +'s between. So accept for example $2916x+4860x^2+2160x^4$
Note that the expansion can be done by $(3+2x)^6=3^6\left(1+\frac{2}{3}x\right)^6$ The unsimplified versions of the terms are: $t(2)=3^6\times6\left(\frac{2}{3}x\right)$, $t(3)=3^6\times\frac{6\times5}{2}\left(\frac{2}{3}x\right)^2$ and $t(5)=3^6\times\frac{6\times5\times4\times3}{4\times3\times2\times1}\left(\frac{2}{3}x\right)^4$
Method using consecutive terms of a GP e.g. $\frac{2160x^4}{4860x^2}=\frac{4860x^2}{2916x}$

A1
M1: Uses the fact that the 2nd, 3rd and 5th terms of their binomial expansion in (a) are consecutive terms of a GP to set up an equation in $x$. There are a few ways in which the equation could be set up so look carefully at what is written. The most common ways are $\frac{"2160x^4"}{"4860x^2"}=\frac{"4860x^2"}{"2916x"}$, and $"2160x^4"="4860x^2"\times"4860x^2"\div"2916x"$. Condone slips e.g. 2196 for 2916. The candidates must be using what they believe are the 2nd, 3rd and 5th terms of the binomial expansion and not the 2nd, 3rd or 4th or any other combination. If a list is given it must be the 2nd, 3rd and 5th terms in $a+bx+cx^2+dx^3+ex^4+\ldots$ where $a,b,c,d\neq0$
dM1: It is dependent on the first M and having the correct index on the powers of $x$. It is for proceeding to an equation of the form $\ldots x=\ldots$
A1: $x=\frac{15}{4}$ or exact equivalent. Condone an extra $x=0$
